implementation_notes: Boost.Signals2 supplies the channel as a signal object: connect() registers a slot (function, lambda, member function or bound expression), calling the signal with its arguments emits to every connected slot, and the returned boost::signals2::connection disconnects deterministically - scoped_connection ties removal to a scope. Slots can be tracked so that a destroyed subscriber is disconnected automatically, which is the C++ answer to listener leaks. The classic hand-rolled registry is still justified only when adding Boost is not an option; Qt's signals/slots are the alternative when the Qt meta-object system is already in the stack.
pitfalls: Slot bodies are not serialised: emitting from several threads runs concurrent slots, so subscriber state needs its own synchronisation.
A connection that is never stored cannot be disconnected, and a captured subscriber stays alive (or dangling) for as long as the signal exists.
Emitting while iterating a slot that disconnects itself is handled by Signals2, but destroying the signal itself during emission is still undefined.

variants.name: Qt signals and slots (meta-object system)
variants.implementation_notes: Qt moves the registry into the meta-object system: a signal is a member function generated by moc, a slot is any invocable, and QObject::connect() wires them with compile-time signature checking on the function-pointer syntax. Connections are removed automatically when the sender or receiver QObject is destroyed, and a lambda connection with a context object inherits the same lifetime rule; queued connections additionally deliver across threads through the receiver's event loop. Choose it when Qt is already the application framework, not as a general C++ event bus.
pitfalls: A class that declares signals must carry Q_OBJECT and be processed by moc; forgetting it yields link errors about the vtable rather than a compile error at the connect site.
Lambda connections without a context object are not disconnected when the receiver dies - pass a context (usually this).
String-based SIGNAL()/SLOT() connections are checked at runtime only: prefer the function-pointer syntax.

variants.name: Hand-rolled std::function subscriber list
variants.implementation_notes: Without a signal library the channel is a vector of std::function slots: subscribe pushes (and returns an id or iterator for removal), publish copies the vector under the mutex and invokes each slot outside the lock so a slot may subscribe or unsubscribe. This is portable to any C++11 toolchain and keeps the dependency surface empty, but registration, snapshotting and lifetime are hand-written, which is exactly the work Boost.Signals2 exists to remove.
pitfalls: Invoking slots while holding the registry mutex deadlocks as soon as a slot subscribes or unsubscribes.
Erasing from the live vector during dispatch invalidates the iteration: snapshot first.
std::function copies the closure: a slot capturing shared state by value silently isolates itself from later mutations.
